findings.title: Duplicate downsize definition breaks existing 4-argument callers
findings.body: The class now defines `downsize` twice (lines 145 and 149). In Ruby the second definition silently overrides the first, so the width/height variant is dead code and any existing caller invoking `OptimizedImage.downsize(from, to, width, height)` now hits the new signature where `dimensions` receives the width integer and `opts` receives the height integer. The dimensions string passed to convert becomes just the width (e.g. "800" instead of "800x600"), producing a malformed ImageMagick resize argument, and opts is a Fixnum so `opts[:allow_animation]` will raise NoMethodError. All existing thumbnail-generation callers of the old API break at runtime.

findings.title: Hardcoded 10MB client limit ignores site settings
findings.body: The client-side upload validation previously used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']` so it matched the server's per-type configured limits. It now hardcodes 10MB for both images and attachments. On sites configured with smaller limits the client will let a file through that the server then rejects, and on sites with larger attachment limits (e.g. max_attachment_size_kb > 10MB) valid uploads are blocked client-side with a wrong error message. This is a functional regression of the configurable limits.

findings.title: 413 error message hardcodes 10MB regardless of server config
findings.body: The 413 handler now reports "10 MB" as the max size instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. When a site has a different max image size configured, the user is shown an incorrect limit in the error dialog, misleading them about what they can upload.

findings.title: API URL download limit raised to hardcoded 10MB bypassing site setting
findings.body: The remote-download size cap for API-provided URLs was `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` and is now a hardcoded 10.megabytes. This applies to all downloads via the API path (including attachments, not just images that will be downsized), so a site that deliberately lowered max_image_size_kb to limit bandwidth/storage exposure now allows API clients to pull up to 10MB per request from arbitrary URLs, defeating the configured limit.

findings.title: Downsize loop can silently fail and oversized image still submitted
findings.body: The loop downsizes to "80%" up to 5 times (max ~33% area reduction) and ignores the return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize`. If conversion fails (e.g. ImageMagick error, unsupported format such as SVG or a corrupted image), the loop runs all 5 attempts on an unmodified file and then `Upload.create_for` is called anyway with the still-oversized tempfile. Also, five 20% steps are frequently insufficient for a genuinely large image (e.g. a 40MB photo with a 1MB limit), so the upload will fail with a generic error after the CPU cost of up to 5 image conversions. The downsize result should be checked and a stronger reduction strategy (e.g. scaling toward the target size directly) used.

findings.title: In-place convert on the same path can corrupt or fail on the source tempfile
findings.body: `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` runs `convert from[0] ... to` with from == to. ImageMagick reads the input fully before writing, so this usually works, but for animated GIFs the animated path uses gifsicle reading and writing the same file, and any partial write failure leaves the tempfile in a corrupted/truncated state that is then passed to Upload.create_for, potentially producing a broken stored upload. Writing to a separate temp file and replacing the original would be safe.

findings.title: Downsized file keeps original extension/content_type even when format changes
findings.body: After downsizing, the file is registered via `Upload.create_for(..., filename, ...)` with the original filename and content_type. If ImageMagick's convert writes a different format than the extension suggests (or the animated path produces a different output), the stored upload's extension, content type, and actual bytes can disagree, which can later break thumbnail generation and cause browsers to mis-handle the file.
